client: I've been really struggling since my mom passed away six months ago. It feels like everyone around me has just... moved on, like it was no big deal, and I'm still stuck in this heavy fog that I can't seem to get out of. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: I'm so glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying right now — this grief, this fog — makes complete sense after losing your mom. Grief doesn't follow anyone else's timeline, and the loneliness of feeling like the world has moved on while you're still in the thick of it can be one of the hardest parts. I'm curious — when you say you feel "stuck," what does a typical day feel like for you right now?

client: Most days I wake up and there's like this split second where everything feels normal, and then it all comes crashing back. I go through the motions — work, eating, whatever — but it's like I'm watching myself from a distance, just doing things automatically without really feeling present. And then at night it gets worse, because that's when the quiet sets in and I start thinking about all the things I never got to say to her.
therapist: That split second you describe — that brief moment of normalcy before the grief rushes back — sounds both like a small mercy and a painful reminder all at once, and it takes real courage to keep showing up to your days even when you're running on autopilot. The nights sound especially hard, and those unspoken words have a way of feeling very heavy in the silence. I'd gently like to explore that with you — when you think about the things you never got to say to her, is there one feeling that tends to surface most strongly?

client: Honestly, the strongest feeling is guilt. Like, I keep replaying conversations where I was impatient with her, or times I didn't call when I said I would, and now I can't fix any of it. It's this constant loop in my head that tells me I wasn't a good enough daughter when it actually mattered.
therapist: That guilt loop sounds absolutely exhausting, and I want to gently offer this — the fact that you're feeling it so deeply speaks to how much you loved her, not to a lack of love when she was here. In CBT, we often notice that our minds in grief can become very selective, replaying the moments we fell short while quietly editing out the countless ways we showed up. If a close friend described her relationship with her mother exactly the way you've described yours, would you look at her and see someone who "wasn't good enough" — or would you see something more complicated and human?

client: I hear what you're saying, and logically I know I'd probably tell a friend that she was human and that nobody's perfect. But when it comes to myself, that logic just doesn't seem to land the same way — it feels like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily, like I don't deserve that kind of understanding. My mom deserved better, and I feel like softening that somehow dishonors how much I failed her.
therapist: What you just named — this sense that self-compassion feels like a betrayal of your mom — is such an important and honest insight, and it's worth sitting with rather than rushing past. I want to gently ask: do you think your mom, who clearly mattered so deeply to you, would have wanted you to sentence yourself to this pain as a way of honoring her love? What do you imagine she would actually say to you right now, if she could?

client: That question actually made me catch my breath for a second, because I know in my heart she would have told me to stop beating myself up. But then there's this other part of me that immediately thinks, well, that's just what she would have said because she loved me, not because I actually deserved it. It's like even imagining her forgiveness, I find a way to argue against it.
therapist: That moment where you caught your breath — that was your heart recognizing something true before your mind could talk you out of it, and I don't want us to move past that too quickly. What you're describing is a really common but painful pattern in CBT — the mind working overtime to block any evidence that might challenge the belief that you're undeserving, essentially moving the goalposts so that no amount of forgiveness, even hers, can ever quite reach you. I'm wondering — what do you think it would mean for you, or what might you have to let go of, if you allowed her forgiveness to actually count?

client: I think if I let her forgiveness actually count, I'd have to let go of the guilt, and the guilt is... it's become this strange way of staying connected to her, like as long as I'm punishing myself I'm still somehow in a relationship with her. Letting it go feels terrifying, almost like losing her a second time. I don't know if I'm ready for that, and I'm not sure I even know who I am in my grief without that weight to carry.
therapist: What you just uncovered is profound — the guilt isn't just punishment, it's become a way of holding onto her, and that makes it feel impossible to release even when it's hurting you. I want you to know that letting go of the guilt doesn't mean letting go of *her* — there are other ways to stay connected to your mom that don't require you to suffer, like honoring what she valued, or carrying forward the love rather than the pain. I'm curious — outside of the guilt, are there any other ways, even small ones, that you already feel her presence or keep her close?

client: There are a few small things, like sometimes I cook the recipes she taught me, and for a moment it feels like she's there in the kitchen with me. But honestly I hadn't really thought of those moments as a way of staying connected — I think I've been so consumed by the guilt that I almost felt like I didn't deserve those softer memories. It's a little scary to consider leaning into those things intentionally, because what if it just makes the missing her even more unbearable?
therapist: Those kitchen moments — her recipes, her presence in something as simple as a meal — that *is* a real, living connection to her, and it's beautiful that you already have that even without fully realizing it. Your fear makes complete sense, but I'd gently offer that the missing her is already there; what those softer memories might actually bring is some warmth alongside the ache, rather than more pain on top of pain. I wonder if this week you might try cooking one of her recipes with a gentle curiosity — not to force anything, but just to notice what comes up — and see if the experience feels different when you approach it as a way of honoring her rather than something you don't deserve?

client: I think I could maybe try that, but I'm a little worried that I'll just end up sitting there crying alone in my kitchen, and then feel worse and more isolated than before. The loneliness is already so heavy, and doing something that was so tied to her without anyone around to share it with feels like it might just highlight how much has changed. I don't really have people in my life right now who knew her the way I did, and that makes everything feel even more solitary.
therapist: The loneliness you're describing — grieving someone when the people around you didn't know her the same way — is its own particular kind of isolation, and it makes complete sense that sharing one of her recipes alone feels daunting rather than comforting right now. Crying in the kitchen isn't necessarily a sign that something went wrong, but I also don't want to push you toward something that feels too solitary too soon — so I'm wondering if there's any way to make that first attempt feel a little less alone, even in a small way, like calling someone while you cook or sharing the finished meal with a neighbor. And I'm also curious — is there anyone in your life, even someone who didn't know your mom well, who you feel safe enough with to start letting them into even a small piece of what you're carrying?

client: There's one friend, Sarah, who has checked in on me a few times, but I keep giving her the "I'm fine" answer because I don't want to be a burden or make things awkward between us. I guess I'm afraid that if I actually tell her how bad it's been, she won't know what to say and then I'll feel even more alone than if I hadn't said anything. It's almost easier to keep people at a distance than to risk that kind of disappointment.
therapist: It's so understandable to want to protect yourself from that risk, and yet I notice that Sarah has checked in *multiple times* — that's someone quietly signaling that she wants to show up for you, even if she doesn't know how heavy things really are. The story your mind is telling you — that honesty will push her away — is worth gently examining, because it might be protecting you from disappointment while also keeping you from the very connection you're aching for. What do you think would actually happen if you gave Sarah just a small, honest answer next time she checked in — not the whole weight of everything, but something a little closer to the truth?

client: Honestly, when I think about it that way, I can see that Sarah probably wouldn't just disappear on me — she's been too consistent for that. But there's still this voice in my head saying that there's a difference between checking in out of obligation and actually being able to handle what I'd share. I think I'd be okay trying something small, like admitting I'm having a harder time than I've let on, but I don't really know how to start that conversation without it feeling forced or dramatic.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can already see Sarah's consistency as evidence that she cares, and that you're open to trying something small — that's not a minor thing, that's a genuine shift. Starting doesn't have to be dramatic or perfectly worded; something as simple as "I've actually been struggling more than I've let on, and I think I needed to finally say that out loud" opens a door without requiring you to walk through the whole story at once. I'm wondering — if you imagine saying something like that to Sarah, what feels like the hardest part: finding the words, or allowing yourself to be seen as someone who isn't okay right now?
